sections.title: Two AI species: rankers and generators
ps: A recommender model answers 'which of these millions of items should this person see next'; a large language model (LLM — a text generator trained on next-word prediction) writes — two different species of AI with fundamentally different compute shapes

Recommenders are memory-bound: their bulk is embedding tables — giant lookup structures translating every user, post, and ad into lists of numbers — terabytes of parameters touched sparsely, so the bottleneck is memory capacity and bandwidth, not arithmetic

LLMs are the inverse: dense matrix math, arithmetic-hungry and predictable in access pattern — which is why hardware ideal for one workload can be mediocre at the other, and why an ads company's first custom chip targeted ranking inference rather than chatbots

Scale flips the intuition about which is 'bigger': serving ranked feeds and ads to billions of users daily can consume more total compute than chatbots do — recommender inference was hyperscale AI years before generative AI made the term famous

sections.title: The economics of giving models away
ps: 'Open weights' means publishing the trained parameters so anyone can run and fine-tune the model; it is not classic open source — the training data and recipe usually stay private, and the license can still restrict the largest competitors

The strategy is commoditizing your complement: if models become cheap commodities, value migrates to what pairs with them — distribution, data, and infrastructure — which favors a company that monetizes attention rather than selling model access

A company with no cloud or API business loses nothing by giving models away — it cannot cannibalize revenue it does not earn — while every rival selling per-token access watches free alternatives compress its prices from below

The side payments are real: open weights recruit researchers who want visible impact, seed an ecosystem of tools built to your architecture, and can make your model line a default standard — industry influence bought at near-zero marginal cost

sections.title: Building compute shelters, not monuments
ps: A traditional data center is a decades-grade concrete building; a tent-style build stretches weatherproof fabric over steel frames around prefabricated power and cooling modules — a structure engineered to be sufficient rather than permanent

The logic is asymmetric depreciation: the GPUs inside may be economically obsolete in about five years while a concrete shell lasts thirty — when the contents wear out faster than the container, paying for container permanence is capital on the wrong asset

Time is the actual currency: when model capability tracks deployed compute, a structure type that shaves quarters off first-power converts directly into training runs a competitor has not even started

The trade-offs are accepted, not ignored: weather exposure, less physical hardening, more operating friction — tolerable for training clusters, which can pause and restart, in a way it never would be for customer-serving clouds bound by uptime contracts

sections.title: The arms-race logic of AI capex
ps: The game-theory structure is a classic dilemma: if rivals build capacity and you do not, you may fall behind irrecoverably; if you build and demand disappoints, you wrote a very large check — that asymmetry pushes every player to build

Executives across the industry reason explicitly in these terms: overbuilding is a recoverable error (assets can be depreciated, repurposed, run below capacity), while being compute-starved during a capability breakthrough might not be recoverable at all

Capacity is also an option contract with physics: owning ready power, land, and shells means you can exercise instantly if the next model generation demands ten times the compute — the capex buys the right to act without multi-year lead times

The brake on the spiral is capital-market patience: when the spending is funded by one profitable core business rather than customer contracts, the market's tolerance — expressed through stock reactions to guidance — is the only external check

sections.title: Engagement data: the labeled dataset nobody can buy
ps: Ranking models learn from labeled examples (supervised learning), and a social platform generates billions of labels daily for free: every click, pause, share, and hide is a human marking what interested them — a self-renewing dataset no budget could purchase

The social graph adds structure raw text lacks: who connects to whom and which content travels across which relationships — signals that sharpen ranking and ad targeting and that exist nowhere outside the platform's own logs

The advantage is workload-specific: engagement data is gold for predicting human preference and attention, but it is not the web-scale text that teaches a language model to reason — a data moat in ranking does not automatically transfer to frontier generative models

The feedback loop cuts both ways: models trained on engagement optimize for engagement, which reshapes what users see and therefore the next round of training data — a closed loop that is simultaneously a competitive asset and the core critique of the medium

sections.title: Green tariffs: renewable buying through your utility
ps: In regulated US states a large customer often cannot sign a power contract directly with a developer — the local utility holds a legal monopoly on selling electricity — so the workaround is a green tariff: a utility-intermediated clean-energy purchase

Mechanics: the utility contracts for (or builds) new renewable and storage projects, and the customer signs a special rate schedule that pays those projects' costs and receives the clean-energy credit — the utility is the middleman that makes the deal legal

The regulator's test is cost containment: tariff structures are publicly reviewed to ensure the data center's dedicated resources are paid for by the data center — the ratepayer-protection question that now shadows every large-load interconnection

Three procurement architectures coexist: direct developer PPAs in deregulated markets, utility green tariffs in regulated ones, and outright asset ownership — most giant buyers end up running all three, matched to each grid's legal structure

flashcards.q: What is an embedding table and why does it make recommender models memory-bound?
flashcards.a: It's a giant lookup structure translating every user, item, and ad into a list of numbers the model can compute with. The tables run to terabytes but each query touches only a few rows — so the bottleneck is memory capacity and bandwidth, not arithmetic speed.

flashcards.q: Why can hardware that's great for LLMs be mediocre for recommenders?
flashcards.a: LLMs are compute-bound: dense, predictable matrix math that keeps arithmetic units saturated. Recommenders are memory-bound: sparse lookups across huge tables. A chip optimized for one profile — lots of math units versus lots of fast memory — underperforms on the other.

flashcards.q: Why was recommender inference 'hyperscale AI' before chatbots existed?
flashcards.a: Serving ranked feeds and ad predictions to billions of users every day consumes enormous total compute — often more than generative chat does. The infrastructure lessons of AI at scale were learned on ranking systems years before LLMs made AI compute famous.

flashcards.q: How do 'open weights' differ from classic open source?
flashcards.a: Open weights publishes the trained parameters so anyone can run and fine-tune the model. But the training data, code, and recipe usually stay private, and the license can restrict the biggest competitors — so you can use the artifact without being able to reproduce it.

flashcards.q: What does 'commoditize your complement' mean as a model strategy?
flashcards.a: Make the adjacent product cheap and abundant so value migrates to what you actually sell. If models become free commodities, advantage shifts to distribution, data, and infrastructure — which suits a company monetizing attention, and undercuts rivals whose revenue is selling model access per token.

flashcards.q: Why can a company without a cloud business afford to give frontier models away?
flashcards.a: It cannot cannibalize revenue it doesn't earn — there's no API or cloud income to lose. Meanwhile the giveaway recruits researchers, seeds a tool ecosystem around its architecture, and pressures competitors' pricing. The strategic cost lands entirely on rivals.

flashcards.q: What is the logic of a tent-style, structure-light data center?
flashcards.a: Asymmetric depreciation: the GPUs inside are obsolete in roughly five years while a concrete shell lasts thirty — so paying for permanence puts capital on the wrong asset. The fabric structure trades weather exposure and hardening for months of saved schedule, tolerable because training clusters can pause.

flashcards.q: Why do training clusters tolerate building compromises that customer-facing clouds cannot?
flashcards.a: A training run can checkpoint, pause, and resume — an interruption costs time, not broken customer promises. A serving cloud is bound by uptime contracts where minutes of outage are measured in penalties and lost trust. Different tolerance for risk, different buildings.

flashcards.q: What asymmetry drives the AI capex arms race?
flashcards.a: Overbuilding is recoverable — assets get depreciated, repurposed, or run below capacity. Falling irrecoverably behind during a capability breakthrough may not be. When every player weighs a bounded loss against an unbounded one, everyone builds — the structure of the game, not exuberance alone, drives the spending.

flashcards.q: In what sense is spare data-center capacity an 'option'?
flashcards.a: Owning ready power, land, and shells is the right — but not the obligation — to scale instantly if the next model generation demands 10x compute. The capex buys freedom from multi-year lead times; like any option, it costs real money and may expire unused.

flashcards.q: What makes engagement data valuable, and what are its limits?
flashcards.a: Every click, pause, and share is a free human label of what interests people — a self-renewing supervised dataset for ranking and ad models that money can't buy. But it's preference data, not the web-scale text that teaches reasoning — the moat doesn't automatically transfer to frontier LLMs.

flashcards.q: How does a utility green tariff work?
flashcards.a: In regulated states where the utility legally must be your power seller, it contracts new renewable and storage projects and the large customer signs a special rate schedule paying those costs and claiming the clean energy. Regulators review the tariff to keep the costs off other ratepayers.
